raw_response.country: Multi-country / global (with focus country syntheses on India, Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Pacific Islands including Fiji and Vanuatu, alongside evaluated studies in Iceland, Germany, South Africa, Uganda, Palau, Bangladesh, Nepal, Canada, and Latin America/Caribbean)

criterion_notes.c1: Fails C1. The systematic review examines Water Safety Plans (WSPs), which are hazard/risk assessment and risk management frameworks aimed at ensuring drinking-water quality and preventing microbial/chemical contamination from catchment to consumer, rather than household or community access to water or sanitation services (Exclusion Criterion 3: water-quality studies that do not examine access).
criterion_notes.c2: Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the review touches on institutional, organizational, and regulatory dimensions of drinking-water quality management (e.g., interagency coordination, utility organizational culture, mandatory WSP drinking-water regulations in Iceland, incentive-based municipal water quality reporting in South Africa, and community water management/tax recovery in an Indian pilot), which could arguably pass plain Criterion 2 in isolation (though the overall study is still excluded under plain_criterion2_decision because it fails C1 and C4). Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading, C2 is clearly 'no': WSP implementation is an operational/technical risk-assessment and water-quality management methodology (modelled on HACCP) accompanied by operator training and hygiene promotion, not a rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing household or community service access (such as eligibility screening, documentation/tenure rules, connection/tariff rules governing access, disconnection/enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure governing access).
criterion_notes.c3: Satisfies C3. The paper is a systematic review of 53 documents (screened from 1,627 initial hits across PubMed, Engineering Village, Google Scholar, and IWA/WHO portals), synthesizing WSP implementation case studies and 24 documents reporting empirical evaluation outcomes and impacts alongside guidance manuals.
criterion_notes.c4: Fails C4. Reported outcomes across the synthesized studies are drinking-water microbiological safety (E. coli detection, sanitary inspection risk scores), compliance with drinking-water quality standards and sampling schedules, utility water-quality monitoring cost savings and return on investment, operational source repair/chlorination/log-keeping, organizational culture, and health outcomes (diarrhoea rates and hospital-acquired infections). It does not evaluate household or community service access, connection, availability, continuity, quantity, household affordability, or exclusion.
criterion_notes.c5: Satisfies C5. Study design (systematic review), units of analysis (water utilities, rural community-managed water supplies, and national/subnational WSP programs across 53 documents), exposure (WSP implementation/adaptation), and outcome categories (institutional, operational, financial, policy/regulatory compliance, and health impacts) are clearly identifiable.
criterion_notes.c6: Satisfies C6. Full text is published in English.

evidence_quotes.quote: The goal of Water Safety Plans (WSPs) is to ensure drinking water safety by preventing or minimizing contamination.

The WHO Guidelines state ‘the most effective means of consistently ensuring the safety of a drinking-water supply is through the use of a comprehensive risk assessment and risk management approach that encompasses all steps in water supply from catchment to consumer.

We conducted a systematic review to collate outcomes, impacts, and lessons learned from WSPs developed in general, rural, and three case-study country contexts. Overall, 53 documents met inclusion criteria.
Another follow-up study by Gunnarsdoittir et al. that tracked water suppliers before and after WSP implementation, found detection of E. coli decreased from 1.28% to 0.32% after WSP implementation

raw_response.exposure: Water Safety Plan (WSP) implementation and local adaptation (5-step risk assessment and risk management framework for drinking-water quality)
raw_response.outcome: Drinking-water quality and microbial contamination (E. coli detection, sanitary risk ratings), compliance with drinking-water quality and sampling regulations, utility monitoring cost savings/ROI, operational source repair and chlorination, utility organizational culture, and health impacts (diarrhoea incidence, hospital infections)
raw_response.population_and_sample: 53 included documents covering urban/general water utilities, hospital water systems, and rural community-managed drinking-water supplies implementing Water Safety Plans
raw_response.rationale: Excluded as E01 (Wrong topic: drinking-water quality risk management rather than water or sanitation service access; also fails C2 and C4). String & Lantagne (2016) systematically review 53 documents on Water Safety Plan (WSP) implementation. WSPs are technical/operational drinking-water contamination risk-assessment and risk-management tools (modelled on HACCP), not rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanisms governing household or community service access (failing C2 under the 2026-10-13 clarification). Furthermore, the review examines drinking-water safety/contamination prevention rather than service access (failing C1) and synthesizes water-quality compliance, microbial contamination, utility monitoring cost, organizational culture, and diarrhoeal health outcomes rather than service access, connection, availability, continuity, affordability, or exclusion outcomes (failing C4; thus excluded under both the narrow and plain readings of Criterion 2).
raw_response.study_design: Systematic literature review (53 included documents comprising WSP manuals/guidelines, case studies, and 24 outcome/impact evaluation documents)
